_comment: Baseline numbers for bin/bench.sh.  Each scenario gets two floors
(mars_parse_MBps and mars_live_MBps) plus a vs-best-other ratio.
If a current measurement falls below the floor, the gate fails.
Tolerances bake observed run-to-run noise (~5-8% headless, ~10% live)
into the floor so the gate doesn't flap on identical code.
Re-baseline: run `bin/bench.sh --update-baseline` after a change
you actually want to lock in.  Re-run cross-terminal numbers via
`bin/measure-other.sh` (now 3-trial median per E5) if the iTerm2 /
Warp comparison drifts.
F gate-lock 2026-05-05 (perf-attack F): clean-machine numbers from
bench-run + measure-other (3-trial), × 0.93 (parse) / 0.90 (live,
ratios) safety margin.  Earlier same-day floors were over-loose due
to godot CPU contention skewing measurements ~30% slower than truth.
These are the *minimum* marspot must hold while A/B/C/D attack work is
ongoing; the targets to break above are tracked outside this repository.

scenarios._l3_note: mars_l3_MBps_min: the SHIPPED path (core -> L3, file-backed scrollback), measured by bin/measure-l3.sh and gated by --full since 2026-08-19.  The probe reports the MINIMUM of its trials, not the median: load can only add time, so the fastest trial is the least-contaminated one.  That change is what made this metric usable on a host with a permanent tenant - one batch read 28.7 / 72.3 / 160.0 MiB/s for the same scenario, where a median reports the tenant and the minimum reports marspot.  Floors are min-of-3 x0.90 taken at load1 4.5: 132.8 / 151.0 / 152.9 / 111.9.  Idle best for reference: 194.5 / 167.8 / 172.1 / 125.4 - three of the four are within noise of the loaded reading, which is the point.  ascii is the exception (147.5 loaded vs 194.5 idle): its trial pushes 134 MB and is the likeliest to catch interference in all three tries.  2026-10-17: mixed relocked to 134.2.  Until then an L3 drained its whole PTY queue before going back to its loop, so the probe's 122x39 resize waited for the end of the cat and most trials ran at the startup 80 columns - a narrower grid and less work per line.  The witness shows it (scrollback.bin 48101192 at 80 columns, 48089054 at 122) and so did the instruction count, which split 160 / 196 per byte between trials of one binary.  The old floors were taken from those 80-column trials.  With the pump bounded the resize lands within 8 ms and every trial runs at the width it asked for; three runs at load1 1.6-2.6 read mixed 154.3 / 149.1 / 150.8, and 149.1 x0.90 is the new floor.  The same binary at 122 columns before the change cost 196 instructions a byte against 160 now.  ascii / cjk / emoji still clear their old floors and were left alone; emoji read 108.2 in one of the three runs with all five trials at exactly 1.24 s, cause not found, 126.6 and 134.2 in the others.

Treat a failure here the way bin/bench-remote.sh's load gate says to: valid when idle, re-measure otherwise.  The job of catching a real regression belongs to mars_l3_MBps_min, which carries the margin. scenarios._note: Relocked 2026-08-18 after the emoji fast-path attack: floor = 135.  Two mini runs an hour apart gave 153.2 (idle) and 145.0 (load1 4.3); 135 is the loaded run x 0.93, so the gate reports a real regression rather than whoever else happens to be compiling on the bench host.  This REPLACES the 2026-07-11 note, whose reasoning was disproved rather than merely outgrown.  That note read: 'pictographic codepoints cannot take the batch lanes (a following VS16/ZWJ changes width), so they pay the segmenter... the honest ceiling is ~66 MB/s'.  The premise is right and the conclusion does not follow: the fast class already guarantees that a batch commit leaves the LAST character buffered, so a following VS16 / ZWJ / skin-tone modifier still meets an OPEN cluster on the slow path and re-decides its width there.  What genuinely cannot be admitted is a character whose boundary depends on a neighbour - regional indicators (GB12/13) and skin-tone modifiers (GBP=Extend) - and those are two ranges, pinned against the tables by `the_fast_pictograph_class_never_outruns_the_tables` over the whole codepoint space.  Measured 61 -> 153.2 MB/s = 2.15x, with ascii / mixed / cjk unchanged or better.  Full decomposition and the per-change prices are in the perf notes.  mars_live_MBps_min for this scenario was re-set on 2026-11-22 from the shipped app's readings (see the top-level _comment).

Floor 35 = the LOWEST of four mini runs x 0.93, the same rule as cat-emoji's.  38 was set first, from a single 40.9 reading, and straddled the noise: four runs at mini load 6.5-8.3 gave 40.9 / 39.8 / 37.9 / 37.3, so the gate failed twice on the same code.  A floor that fires on whoever else is compiling teaches you to relock rather than to look, which is the failure this whole file argues against.  35 still catches the regression this scenario was written to catch: capturing a scrolled-off cluster by COPYING it rather than moving it read 26.1.  Deliberately pathological: real pane output measured 55 multi-codepoint clusters in forty million, so this number is about a code path and not about a workload.  It is ~10% below where the same stream parsed before the cluster pool existed (47.9 -> 42.8 MB/s on the dev box, three runs each), which is what holding a cluster whole costs when a third of the stream is clusters.

render_full_repaint._comment: p99 across 1000 iterations × median of 3 trials.  Real-world swing on a hot mac is up to ~2 ms (observed range 1.0-1.4 ms across one day's bench runs — 30 % spread driven by GPU thermal + scheduler noise).  Ceiling at 1.8 ms catches an actual regression (1.5x current median) while tolerating that noise.  --update-baseline applies the default 1.10 margin which collapses to the noise floor; manually widened.

scroll_repaint._comment: p99 ns/repaint while walking view_offset from 5000 -> 0 in 3-line steps over 100K-line scroll-history.bin (--bench scroll).  Picks up MARS_DISK_SCROLLBACK so the gate tracks whichever variant is current default.  Median of 5 trials.  Relocked 2026-07-11: 10-sample idle-mini distribution is 3000-3125ns, median 3083ns, stdev ~1% (timer quantum ~41ns) - the old floor 3 was set as 2x a ~1.5us median and never re-widened; same-binary historical readings spanned 1.8-3.1us so no regression vs Jun-6 is provable from available data.  Floor = 3.083 x 1.3 (the 30% margin scroll convention, matching scroll_cold) = 4.  A real >30% scroll regression still fails the gate.

scroll_cold_repaint._comment: Sister gate to scroll_repaint, forced to disk-backed (MARS_DISK_SCROLLBACK=1) and with pages evicted via madvise(DONTNEED) before the walk.  Catches disk-path regressions that the default-env scroll bench misses when memory is the default.  Cold-cache p99 measured ~3-5 µs; same 30 % run-to-run noise as the warm gate, manually widened to ~2x current median.

key_to_frame._comment: 2026-11-22: microseconds from a key event's timestamp to the shell's present call returning, one pane in a 1000x760 pt window, 200 keys a run (runs of 20 `x` then 20 backspaces, 120-150 ms apart), bin/measure-latency.sh scene type-1 inside `bin/bench.sh --full`; the figure is the median over runs 2-4 of each run's percentile (p99 of 200 keys is the third-largest, so the one slow key every run has, 16-27 ms max, does not reach it).  Shell and core are a latency-trace build, the session the shipped binary.  Mini, M4 Pro, macOS 27.2.1, load1 1.3-3.6, commit 7b2701b plus this gate: test-e2e-remote run, 5 rounds: p50 2862 / 2972 / 2944 / 2964 / 2889, p99 3586 / 3863 / 3675 / 3932 / 3882; bench-remote --full run 20261121T220401Z, runs 1-4: p50 2904 / 2977 / 2924 / 2861, p99 3844 / 3709 / 3957 / 3804.  Ceilings = worst reading x margin: p99 3957 x 1.30 = 5144 -> 5150, p50 2977 x 1.20 = 3572 -> 3575 (the p50 spreads 4 % across nine runs, the p99 10 %).  Both gate: the p50 shows a shift every key pays, which a per-run p99 of 200 keys reads through more noise.  Where the p50 goes (2026-11-22, run r1 above): about 1.2 ms of it is the core finding the GPU done, of which 0.15 ms is GPU work and the rest its 1 ms poll; 0.57 ms build + encode + commit; 0.4-0.7 ms the session's round trip; 0.19 ms the shell's present.  A key whose frame was presented after the next key was pressed (over 120 ms) is left out of the percentiles by bin/_latency_report.py, so the gate counts such keys in a row of its own with a ceiling of 0; a run that stopped part way, fewer reports than runs, or a key never followed to a present make every key-to-frame row invalid rather than read from what is left.

binary_size_bytes_max._comment: 2026-11-22: the gate watches the shipped binaries.  `mcli` and the single-process `marspot` app were deleted; the `marspot` binary that is left holds only the headless benches and ships in no bundle, so its size says nothing about the product.  Ceilings = mini-measured release size + one 16 KiB page, the rule below: marspot-core 2291472 -> 2307856, marspot-session 1504928 -> 1521312 (mini, 2026-11-22, `cargo build --release`, lto=fat, commit 8c700fd).  marspot-shell and marspot-peer carry no ceiling yet.  Everything below is the history of the two retired keys, kept for its findings about page quanta.  Release binary size ceiling (after lto=fat strip).  Purpose: flag ACCIDENTAL code-size jumps (a heavy dep sneaking in, a forgotten debug table) - NOT a hard product budget.  RESOLUTION: on arm64 macOS the __TEXT segment is 16 KiB page-aligned, so these numbers move in ~16 KiB steps whatever the source change was - 2026-08-11 a ~2 KB chrome-layout change (measured: __text +2036 B, every other section flat) grew mcli by 16512 B = one page + 128 B of code signature.  A jump under ~20 KiB says nothing; read the section table (`size -m`) before calling it bloat.  Relocked 2026-08-11 at mini-measured current x 1.06 (one page of headroom, not a percentage): mcli 1375488, marspot 1515840.  marspot came DOWN 34 KB in the same commit by moving `--snapshot` + the PNG writer behind the `snapshot` cargo feature - a development tool has no business in the shipped binary.  Previous ceilings 1370000/1541000 dated 2026-07-11.  NB: measure on the canonical bench host (idle mini); dev-box toolchains can differ.  Relocked 2026-08-12 (marspot only): 1533000 -> 1549776 = mini-measured 1533392 + one 16 KiB page.  The old ceiling sat 72 B above the then-current build - zero headroom - so the next ordinary commit tripped it: a same-machine A/B minutes apart (git stash) showed __TEXT UNCHANGED at 1245184 and __text +3548 B absorbed inside the page, with the 464 B file delta living in linkedit + signature.  That is the sub-page noise this comment already says to ignore, and a floor that fires on it teaches you to relock rather than to look.  mcli's ceiling already carried exactly one page of headroom (1392000 vs 1376160); marspot's now matches the same rule.  Relocked 2026-08-18 (marspot only): 1549776 -> 1567136 = mini-measured 1550752 + one 16 KiB page.  The emoji fast-path commit moved the binary by exactly 16512 B - one page plus 128 B of signature, the same quantum this comment records for 2026-08-11 - i.e. the sub-page noise it already says to ignore.  Relocked 2026-08-19: mcli 1392000 -> 1452592, marspot 1567136 -> 1626608 (mini-measured + one 16 KiB page).  Both grew ~43 KB in one commit range, which is past the ~20 KB this comment says to ignore, so it was read rather than waved through: the growth is the `async_writer` module plus the reworked scrollback and bytelog paths, and it bought 2.9-4.8x on the shipped path.  Relocked 2026-09-07: mcli 1452592 -> 1471968, marspot 1626608 -> 1646720 (mini-measured 1455584 / 1630336 + one 16 KiB page).  The local-echo expiry commit tripped both by 2992 / 3728 B - under the ~20 KB this comment says to ignore, so the section table was read first: same-machine A/B (git stash) shows __TEXT UNCHANGED at 1179648 with __text +872 B, __const +96 B, __cstring +109 B absorbed inside the page; the file delta lives in linkedit + signature.  Sub-page noise, and both ceilings had under 3 KB of headroom left.  NOT relocked 2026-09-08, and the near-miss is worth recording: the Codex-accounts commit tripped both ceilings by 18224 / 18176 B and the section table said one 16 KiB __TEXT page carrying __text +4640 B and __const +3992 B.  A follow-up commit that only lower-cased the panel's window labels put __TEXT back to 1327104 — UNCHANGED from before the feature — leaving the whole feature at __text +112 B, __cstring -132 B, and both binaries under the existing ceilings (mini-measured 1456640 / 1631424 vs 1471968 / 1646720).  Same on the dev box, byte for byte.  The ~8.6 KB was then chased down with a symbol-level diff of two unstripped builds (`strip = "debuginfo"` keeps the table, so plain `nm` is enough): it is `alloc::str::to_lowercase` — 3348 B of code that drags in the Final_Sigma rule (a Greek capital sigma lower-cases to ς at the end of a word), which needs the Cased and Case_Ignorable properties, hence `unicode_data::{case_ignorable, lowercase, uppercase, lt}` bitsets: 2270 + 1712 + 919 + 456 + 352 + 320 + 304 + 268 B, all present ONLY in the upper-case build.  `str::to_uppercase` has no context-sensitive rule and costs nothing comparable.  The upper-case cut called `to_lowercase` from inside the PAINTER (to lower-case each label for its timeline tag), and the painter is reachable from every binary; the lower-case cut left the only calls in `cc_usage`, which is dead code in `marspot` and `mcli`.  Acting on that finding, the two feed-label conversions moved to `to_ascii_lowercase` (model names out of a JSON feed are ASCII by construction), which took the same 17776 B back out of `marspot-core` — the binary that actually draws the panel and is NOT one of the two this ceiling watches.  Rule of thumb worth keeping: `str::to_lowercase` costs ~9 KB the first time a binary reaches it, `to_ascii_lowercase` costs nothing, and case-folding ASCII data with the Unicode one buys only the sigma rule.  The lesson that does hold: a ceiling trip of ~18 KB can be one page of alignment around a few hundred bytes of real change, and relocking before reading the section table would have raised both ceilings 34 KB above what the shipped build actually needs. competitors_snapshot._comment: Per-terminal version + captured_at. Each entry self-describes when and against what version it was measured, so a snapshot that drifts (one terminal refreshed today, another stuck at an older date) is auditable. `host` describes the bench host all measurements were taken on. bench.sh `vs-best-other` iterates entries with *_MBps keys; `host` / `_comment` are skipped automatically (no key match). terminal.app excluded from the denominator by design (OS-vendor reference floor, not a competitor).  2026-08-18: ghostty + marspot re-measured under a NEW protocol and are NOT comparable with the 2026-06-07 rows above them.  Two changes: (1) every terminal now pushes LIVE_MIN_BYTES (32 MiB) by cat'ing the scenario file as many times as needed — a single 8 MiB pass never blocks `cat` long enough to measure a fast terminal, and the old rows mix per-scenario byte counts; (2) each trial ends with a DSR round-trip (`CSI 6 n`), so the number covers work the terminal has CONFIRMED it consumed.  Without (2) a terminal that drops or coalesces under pressure finishes early and wins — the reason marspot grew DSR support the same day (L2 0.12.138).  iterm/warp/terminal cannot be driven from an ssh session (AppleEvent -1712 under both plain ssh and launchctl asuser for iTerm); they need a console run of bin/measure-other.sh and are stale until then.

multi_session_l3._comment: Nine marspot-session processes absorbing the same scenario at once, run by the gate itself (bin/measure-l3.sh --sessions 9).  insn_per_byte_max judges the LOWEST of the trials: instructions summed over the nine sessions, divided by the bytes they absorbed together.  One session alone costs about 181 per byte on this scenario; nine at once cost 193-368 from trial to trial, depending on how much they get in each other's way, and that difference is what this row shows.  Nine runs of one build read a minimum of 192.61-227.85 (range 17 %; the trials inside one run span far more), ceiling = worst x 1.05.  It therefore cannot see a change smaller than about a quarter; the single-session rows are the ones that see 5 %.  The aggregate wall-clock rate (112-130 MB/s best trial in the same runs) is reported and does not gate.  Since readers in bulk output take turns, two at a time (2026-11-12), four runs of one build read 209.50-210.45 and carried 220-223 MB/s together; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  Without the turns the same reader costs 234 a byte here, so this row sees them go missing.  With bulk output handed over in full chunks, four runs read 137.02-137.28 and 263-266 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  With text written to the row in one pass and a scrolled row blanked by one copy (2026-11-12, evening), four runs read 108.14-108.43 and 276-278 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.  With the frame gate, the ring of records, the larger hand-overs to the writer threads and the probe starting its sessions at the pane's size (2026-11-12, night), four runs read 94.42-94.55 and 297-302 MB/s; ceiling = worst x 1.05.

app_footprint_12_panes._comment: Summed phys_footprint of marspot-shell + marspot-core + all 12 marspot-session processes, one window of 4 x 3 panes, each pane printing 40 lines and sitting at a /bin/sh prompt, read once all 12 pane shells run, a frame is on screen and the processes together use under 0.02 of a core over 2 s (bin/measure-app-footprint.sh, run by bin/bench.sh --full inside the console session).  The gate judges the median of the rounds in KiB.  Ceiling from mini 2026-11-22, two runs, 8 rounds: 88710368 to 89152688 bytes (about 84.6 to 85.0 MiB: shell 22.6-22.9, core 38.1-38.3, sessions 1.95-2.05 MiB each, 23.8-24.1 together).  Worst 89152688 B = 87063 KiB, x 1.05 = 91417 KiB.  The rounds agree within 0.5 %, so 5 % is about 4.3 MiB: a session growing by a third of a MiB, or the shell or core by a tenth of itself, trips it.

app_startup._comment: Milliseconds from exec of marspot-shell (sandbox, the shipped three processes, one window of one pane) to the core's WINDOW_FIRST_CONTENT: the shell reported shown the first frame in which the pane shows what its shell printed (bin/measure-startup.sh, run by bin/bench.sh --full in the console session).  cold = first launch of copies signed again ad hoc under a fresh identifier (new inode, new code hash); warm = the same copies launched again right after; the gate judges the median of the trials.  Mini 2026-11-22, two runs: cold 250 163 180 168 163 (median 168, load1 about 2) and 181 156 175 164 160 176 178 (median 175, load1 4-7); warm 144 157 163 147 168 (157) and 179 164 158 157 170 163 171 (164).  Of the time, about 65 ms is before the core is spawned and 35-50 ms is the session's boot.  Cold and warm differ by about 10 ms, inside the spread of either: on mini a never-seen code hash costs nothing measurable at first exec, so the cold row does not yet show a first-launch cost of its own.  Both gate: run medians agreed within 5 % with the host at load 2 and at load 7, so a ceiling of the worst median x 1.5 (cold 175 -> 263, warm 164 -> 246) leaves the host's noise far below the line and still catches a startup that grows by half.

pane_control._comment: P95 in ms of the pane control socket's latencies, each from the request leaving the probe to its answer arriving, on connections kept open and paced under the per-caller rate (bin/measure-pane-control.sh + bin/_pane_control_probe.py, run by bin/bench.sh --full in the console session; one window, a pane reading its input silently and a pane at a /bin/sh prompt).  send: one byte without Enter, answered once written to the PTY.  send_enter: the same with Enter, including the 50 ms the session leaves for the echo.  fired: a `change` wait, from the answer to the send that makes the shell echo to the answer to the wait.  run_true: pane.run true, to the answer with its exit status; runs paced 200 ms apart: input to a pane within 2 s of a run's end there first waits for a prompt watch (shell in front, 150 ms quiet), which a prompt drawn by then answers at once.  run_after_run: the same with each run sent as soon as the one before answered, so it includes that prompt wait.  read: pane.read without history (asks the session nothing, answers no pos). Mini 2026-11-23 after the next input after a run started waiting for the prompt watch instead of a fixed 150 ms, one run at load1 8 (over the reading limit, so the numbers are high if anything): send 1.011, send_enter 60.996, fired 1.575, run_true 5.666, run_after_run 162.624, read 1.131; the earlier ceilings hold, run_after_run gets its first.  Ceiling = the worse run's P95 x 3.  open_shadow: pane.open of a shadow pane to the answer of a `true` run in it, six opens paced 10.5 s apart under the per-parent rate of new panes (6 a minute; ten at once had the probe refused and stop).  Mini 2026-11-23 with PaneControlCaps bit 1 (develop 9be1053 plus the probe pacing), two runs at load1 12.7 and 3.1: send 1.48 / 1.211, send_enter 61.469 / 61.579, fired 1.959 / 1.797, run_true 5.667 / 5.193, run_after_run 162.88 / 162.878, read 1.408 / 1.536, open_shadow 76.952 / 78.644; the earlier ceilings hold, open_shadow gets 3 x 78.644 = 235.9 (the design budget is 500).
